findings.title: `order` mixin emits invalid prefixed properties: `-ms-flex-order` and `-webkit-order` are not valid CSS
findings.body: The `order` mixin (lines 125-131) emits five properties: `-webkit-box-ordinal-group`, `-moz-box-ordinal-group`, `-ms-flex-order`, `-webkit-order`, and `order`. Two of these are invalid: (1) `-ms-flex-order` — the correct IE10 flexbox property is `-ms-flex-order` only in the context of the old 2009/2012 IE flexbox implementation, but the standard IE10 property for the 2012 spec is `-ms-flex-order` is actually correct for IE10... however, `-webkit-order` (line 129) is NOT a valid property — WebKit never shipped a prefixed `order` property; Safari supported unprefixed `order` from the start of its flexbox implementation (Safari 6.1+/7 with `-webkit-flex`). Similarly, `-moz-box-ordinal-group` is for the old 2009 Firefox flexbox (`display: -moz-box`), which is fine as a fallback, but `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` correctly maps to old WebKit flexbox. The real issue: `-webkit-order` is invalid and will be dropped by browsers, and more importantly, `-ms-flex-order` expects an integer but the mixin passes `$val` directly — for the header use case `@include order(3)`, IE10's `-ms-flex-order` uses 1-based ordinal groups where the default is 0, so `order(3)` in IE10 would place the panel after items with default order 0, which may not match the intended visual order of 1,2,3 in modern browsers. The mixin also lacks `-ms-flex-item-align` or other IE10-specific corrections. Invalid properties in the output CSS increase stylesheet size and can confuse CSS validators/linters; the IE10 ordinal mismatch can cause the header panel to appear in the wrong position in IE10.

findings.title: `align-items` mixin emits both `-ms-flex-align` and `-ms-align-items` — `-ms-align-items` is invalid
findings.body: The `align-items` mixin (lines 117-123) emits `-ms-flex-align` (correct for IE10) and `-ms-align-items` (line 121). The property `-ms-align-items` is not a valid CSS property — IE10 only supports `-ms-flex-align` for the 2012 flexbox spec; there is no `-ms-align-items` prefixed property. This invalid property will be ignored by browsers, adding dead weight to the compiled CSS. It should be removed. Additionally, the mixin emits `-webkit-box-align` (for old 2009 flexbox) which expects different keyword values (e.g., `start`, `end`, `center`, `baseline`, `stretch`) — passing `center` works for both old and new specs, but `baseline` in old Webkit flexbox has different behavior; however, since the only usage in this PR is `align-items(center)` and `align-items(baseline)`, the `baseline` value in `-webkit-box-align` (line 118) may render differently in old Safari (6.0) versus modern browsers, potentially causing vertical misalignment of bullet badges in `badges.css.scss` line 57.

findings.title: `@include order(3)` on `.panel` assumes sibling order values 1 and 2 exist, but no other flex items have explicit order — visual order may not match DOM order intent
findings.body: The diff adds `@include order(3)` to `.panel` (line 39) and relies on `margin-left: auto` to push it right. In flexbox, `order` changes the visual ordering of flex items. The default `order` value is 0 for all flex items. By setting `.panel` to `order: 3`, it will be placed after all items with `order: 0` (the default) — which includes `.title`, `.icons`, `.login-button`, etc. — regardless of their DOM position. This means `.panel` will always render last among the flex items, which may be the intent (pushing the user panel to the right). However, combined with `margin-left: auto`, the behavior is redundant and potentially conflicting: `margin-left: auto` on a flex item absorbs free space and pushes the item (and subsequent items) to the right, but `order: 3` already places it last. If there are other flex items after `.panel` in the DOM with default `order: 0`, they would appear BEFORE `.panel` visually despite being after it in the DOM — this is an accessibility concern (visual order ≠ DOM order, confusing screen reader users) and may cause unexpected layout if the header DOM structure changes. The `order` property should be used sparingly; using `margin-left: auto` alone would achieve the right-alignment without reordering.

findings.title: Replacing raw `display: inline-flex` with `@include inline-flex()` adds old-spec fallbacks that change rendering in legacy browsers
findings.body: The diff replaces `display: inline-flex; align-items: baseline;` (raw modern CSS) with `@include inline-flex()` and `@include align-items(baseline)` (lines 55-57). The `inline-flex()` mixin (mixins.scss lines 108-114) emits `display: -webkit-inline-box; display: -webkit-inline-flex; display: -moz-inline-box; display: -ms-inline-flexbox; display: inline-flex;`. The old-spec fallbacks `-webkit-inline-box` and `-moz-inline-box` use the 2009 flexbox model, which has different sizing and alignment behavior than modern flexbox. In old Safari (6.0) and old Firefox (pre-22), the badge wrapper will render using the 2009 box model, where `align-items: baseline` (via `-webkit-box-align: baseline`) behaves differently — specifically, baseline alignment in old flexbox aligns to the first line of text, which may cause the bullet badge's colored dot and category text to misalign vertically compared to modern browsers. Since the original code used unprefixed `inline-flex` (which old browsers simply ignore, falling back to the `display: inline-block` from `.badge-wrapper` line 22), the visual result in old browsers was a simple inline-block badge. The mixin change makes old browsers attempt flexbox layout with the old spec, potentially introducing visual bugs in legacy browsers that were previously rendering correctly with inline-block fallback.
